Equinix has not yet filed or reported **Q3 2026** as of October 17, 2026: its investor-relations filing page identifies the latest quarterly filing as the **Q2 2026 Form 10-Q**, filed July 29, 2026, while Q3 earnings are scheduled for October 28, 2026. [[1, 2]] 

In the latest reported quarter, **Q2 2026 (three months ended June 30, 2026)**, Equinix generated **$2.625 billion of total revenue**, up **16% year over year** from **$2.256 billion**. [[3, 4]]

| Q2 2026 segment result | Revenue ($m) | Recurring revenue ($m) | Non-recurring revenue ($m) | Segment adjusted EBITDA ($m) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Americas | 1,251 | 1,067 | 184 | 641 |
| EMEA | 845 | 806 | 39 | 456 |
| Asia-Pacific | 529 | 504 | 25 | 299 |
| **Total** | **2,625** | **2,377** | **248** | **1,396** |

The figures above are from Equinix’s Q2 2026 Form 10-Q, which defines the company’s three reportable geographic segments as Americas, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific and reports revenue and adjusted EBITDA by segment. [[4]] 

Americas was the largest and fastest-growing segment, with revenue up **$247 million, or 25% year over year**, to $1.251 billion; EMEA revenue rose **$78 million, or 10%**, to $845 million; and Asia-Pacific revenue rose **$44 million, or 9%**, to $529 million. [[4]] 

For context only, Equinix’s Q2 release guided to **Q3 2026 revenue of $2.525 billion to $2.575 billion**, rather than reporting a Q3 actual result. [[3]]

tool_arguments.query: Equinix AI-related data-center leasing xScale demand Q2 2026 or recent earnings call transcript

events.content: Equinix AI-related data-center leasing xScale demand Q2 2026 or recent earnings call transcript

**Q2 2026 takeaway:** Equinix characterized demand as broad-based and stronger than its prior long-term planning assumptions, with demand split between large enterprises modernizing legacy on-premises infrastructure and net-new AI-native workloads/service providers. [[1]]

- Equinix closed **134 MW of xScale leases** in Q2 2026, including the Hampton transaction, which generated roughly **$120 million of non-recurring fees**. [[1]]
- Management said **“the vast majority” of its largest Q2 deals were driven by AI workloads**, consistent with the prior several quarters. [[1]]
- Importantly, the company did **not** disclose that all 134 MW of xScale leasing was AI-specific; the more supportable reading is that AI is a major demand accelerant across its portfolio, while xScale leasing activity includes hyperscale capacity transactions such as Hampton. [[1]]
- The strength translated into a capacity-response plan: Equinix added nine projects since April and had **52 projects underway across 33 markets** at quarter-end. [[2]]
- Q2 revenue was **$2.625 billion**, up **16% year over year**, with growth aided by underlying execution and one-time xScale fees. [[3]]
- Management’s practical demand signal was raised outlook and an accelerated expansion program, with long-term annual capex envisioned at **$5 billion–$7 billion**, excluding real-estate acquisitions and xScale. [[1]]

**Bottom line:** The transcript supports a bullish AI-led leasing thesis—AI drove most large deals and is helping sustain capacity demand—but it does not support equating the full 134 MW of Q2 xScale leases directly to AI demand. [[1]]

tool_arguments.query: Federal Reserve interest rate impact on data-center REITs sector performance 2025 2026 earnings call transcript

events.content: Federal Reserve interest rate impact on data-center REITs sector performance 2025 2026 earnings call transcript

**Bottom line:** Federal Reserve policy was an important valuation and financing variable for data-center REITs in 2025–26, but it did not determine sector returns by itself: exceptional AI/cloud leasing demand and backlog conversion increasingly outweighed rate sensitivity in 2026. [[1]]

**Rate backdrop.** The fed-funds target range began 2025 at 4.25%–4.50%, was lowered to 3.50%–3.75% at the December 9–10, 2025 FOMC meeting, and stood at 3.75%–4.00% after the Fed’s September 2026 increase. [[2]] [[3]] [[4]] This path reduced the short-rate burden versus early 2025, but 2026’s renewed tightening—and persistently elevated long-term funding costs—limited the simple “rate cuts equal REIT upside” narrative. [[5]] [[4]]

**Sector performance versus operating performance.** Data-center REIT total performance was weak in 2025, at **-14.2%**, even though the sector generated **21.3% year-over-year FFO growth** and **7.2% NOI growth** in 1Q25. [[1]] [[6]] That divergence indicates that investors discounted the sector for capital-intensity, required returns, and financing/valuation risk rather than a deterioration in underlying occupancy or demand. [[1]] [[6]] By mid-2026, data centers had become one of the best-performing REIT property types, with a **33.2%** return, while 1Q26 sector FFO and NOI grew **29.4%** and **15.8%**, respectively. [[1]] In other words, the 2026 rerating was supported principally by accelerating cash-flow fundamentals and AI demand, with the less restrictive 2025 rate level acting as a helpful, but not sufficient, tailwind. [[1]]

**How rates transmit to the sector.** Higher risk-free rates can lower REIT equity values through higher discount rates and can compress development spreads by raising the cost of debt and equity needed to build power-intensive capacity. [[7]] [[8]] The effect is especially relevant for data-center REITs because the current investment cycle requires very large up-front development expenditures before facilities stabilize and cash rent commences. [[9]] [[7]] Conversely, lower borrowing rates would improve incremental project economics, refinancing costs, and relative dividend attractiveness, although companies with fixed-rate debt do not receive the full benefit immediately. [[10]]

**Digital Realty: earnings-call and balance-sheet evidence.** Digital Realty reported **$18.4 billion** of total debt at December 31, 2025, net debt/adjusted EBITDA of **4.9x**, and fixed-charge coverage of **4.5x**; it expected 2026  …[truncated]

Related coverage:
**Bottom line:** Federal Reserve tightening is generally a valuation headwind for data-center REITs, while easing is generally supportive, because policy-rate surprises have historically had economically meaningful negative effects on equity REIT prices; one study estimates an unexpected 25-basis-point Fed cut is associated with roughly a 2% rise in U.S. equity-REIT prices on average. [[1]]

**The primary valuation channel is the required return.** A data-center REIT’s enterprise value is commonly framed as stabilized property NOI divided by a cap rate, or as the present value of future cash flows discounted at a required return; higher risk-free rates and often wider credit/equity risk premiums raise those required returns, pushing values lower if NOI is unchanged. [[2]] [[1]]

**Cap-rate sensitivity is especially material because the sector begins from low yields.** Data-center REITs were reported at an implied cap rate of about 4.4% in 2025, the lowest among major REIT property sectors; holding NOI constant, a 50-basis-point move from 4.4% to 4.9% reduces the simple NOI/cap-rate value by about 10.2%. [[3]] [[4]]

**Rates also affect the cost and availability of growth capital.**

private_messages.content:
**Bottom line:** Federal Reserve policy was an important valuation and financing variable for data-center REITs in 2025–26, but it did not determine sector returns by itself: exceptional AI/cloud leasing demand and backlog conversion increasingly outweighed rate sensitivity in 2026. [[1]]

**Rate backdrop.** The fed-funds target range began 2025 at 4.25%–4.50%, was lowered to 3.50%–3.75% at the December 9–10, 2025 FOMC meeting, and stood at 3.75%–4.00% after the Fed’s September 2026 increase. [[2]] [[3]] [[4]] This path reduced the short-rate burden versus early 2025, but 2026’s renewed tightening—and persistently elevated long-term funding costs—limited the simple “rate cuts equal REIT upside” narrative. [[5]] [[4]]

**Sector performance versus operating performance.** Data-center REIT total performance was weak in 2025, at **-14.2%**, even though the sector generated **21.3% year-over-year FFO growth** and **7.2% NOI growth** in 1Q25. [[1]] [[6]] That divergence indicates that investors discounted the sector for capital-intensity, required returns, and financing/valuation risk rather than a deterioration in underlying occupancy or demand. [[1]] [[6]] By mid-2026, data centers had become one of the best-performing REIT property types, with a **33.2%** return, while 1Q26 sector FFO and NOI grew **29.4%** and **15.8%**, respectively. [[1]] In other words, the 2026 rerating was supported principally by accelerating cash-flow fundamentals and AI demand, with the less restrictive 2025 rate level acting as a helpful, but not sufficient, tailwind. [[1]]

**How rates transmit to the sector.** Higher risk-free rates can lower REIT equity values through higher discount rates and can compress development spreads by raising the cost of debt and equity needed to build power-intensive capacity. [[7]] [[8]] The effect is especially relevant for data-center REITs because the current investment cycle requires very large up-front development expenditures before facilities stabilize and cash rent commences. [[9]] [[7]] Conversely, lower borrowing rates would improve incremental project economics, refinancing costs, and relative dividend attractiveness, although companies with fixed-rate debt do not receive the full benefit immediately. [[10]]

**Digital Realty: earnings-call and balance-sheet evidence.** Digital Realty reported **$18.4 billion** of total debt at December 31, 2025, net debt/adjusted EBITDA of **4.9x**, and fixed-charge coverage of **4.5x**; it expected 2026  …[truncated]

Related coverage:
**Bottom line:** Federal Reserve tightening is generally a valuation headwind for data-center REITs, while easing is generally supportive, because policy-rate surprises have historically had economically meaningful negative effects on equity REIT prices; one study estimates an unexpected 25-basis-point Fed cut is associated with roughly a 2% rise in U.S. equity-REIT prices on average. [[1]]

**The primary valuation channel is the required return.** A data-center REIT’s enterprise value is commonly framed as stabilized property NOI divided by a cap rate, or as the present value of future cash flows discounted at a required return; higher risk-free rates and often wider credit/equity risk premiums raise those required returns, pushing values lower if NOI is unchanged. [[2]] [[1]]

**Cap-rate sensitivity is especially material because the sector begins from low yields.** Data-center REITs were reported at an implied cap rate of about 4.4% in 2025, the lowest among major REIT property sectors; holding NOI constant, a 50-basis-point move from 4.4% to 4.9% reduces the simple NOI/cap-rate value by about 10.2%. [[3]] [[4]]

**Rates also affect the cost and availability of growth capital.**
